title: In the beginning (Genesis 1:1–5)
hook: the earth without form, the Spirit over the waters, and the first word: let there be light

segments.voice: Yesterday, the big lookout: the end of year one, the whole climb behind you, and your line was the hill goes on. Did you put your one line somewhere you'd see it this morning? Day three hundred thirty-two.

Open almost any Bible in the world, in any language, and the first page starts the same way. Before kings, before prophets, before a manger or a cross, there are three words in English that most people could finish for you: in the beginning. Year one walked the hill in pieces: words, stories, practices, one Gospel, the depths. Year two does something different. It reads the whole book, in order, from the first line. Not every verse, but every turn of the road. And the road starts somewhere strange: in the dark, over deep water, before there's anything to see at all.
screen: `THE SAME FIRST PAGE, EVERY LANGUAGE.` → `YEAR TWO: THE WHOLE BOOK, IN ORDER.` → `IT STARTS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible the first verse reads: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In Hebrew that whole opening phrase, in the beginning, is one word: bereshit. Jews still call the whole book by it. Then verse two sets the scene, and it isn't tidy: "And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep." Without form, and void, in Hebrew tohu va-vohu, a pair of words that sound like a shrug. Waste and empty. A blank. But it isn't only empty, because the same verse goes on: "And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The Hebrew word for Spirit, ruach, also means wind and breath. Some readers picture a bird hovering over a nest. Something is about to happen. And then, up close, the first thing we see God do is speak. "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." No struggle, no battle, no raw material wrestled into shape. A word, and light. God calls the light day and the darkness night, and the evening and the morning are the first day. Here's the strange part: the sun doesn't arrive until day four. Light comes first, before anything that shines. Christians have read that in many ways, from a literal week to a poem about order coming out of chaos, and churches hold different views on how it fits with the science of the universe. What they share is the opening claim: the world isn't an accident God stumbled into. And Christians hear these words again at the start of John's Gospel: in the beginning was the Word.
screen: `BERESHIT: IN THE BEGINNING.` · `WITHOUT FORM, AND VOID.` · `THE SPIRIT OVER THE WATERS.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · then, large: `LET THERE BE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch light come or go. Settle, and breathe. Notice where the light in this room is coming from right now: a window, a lamp, a screen. Close your eyes for a few breaths and see the dark behind your eyelids, the deep before anything. Then open them slowly, and let the light come back in, as if for the first time. If you pray, you can say the first line of the Bible quietly. If you don't, just watch the light arrive. The bell holds the time.
In the beginning. Bereshit in Hebrew, the first word of the Bible and the name of its first book, where everything starts with a word and light.
Your line: let there be light. Today, watch one moment when light comes or goes: a sunrise, a sunset, a switch flicked on in a dark room. Day three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Christians read Genesis 1 at the start of a Bible-in-a-year plan, and many churches read it at the Easter Vigil, where the story of creation is one of the first readings of the night.

fork.setup: the earth is without form and void, darkness over the deep. in the story, what is the first thing God does?
options: fights a sea monster to shape the world.
fork.reveal: a word, and light. no struggle, no battle. the sun doesn't come until day four.

original.note: Hebrew: in the beginning, one word, the first in the Bible and the Jewish name for Genesis.

trapdoor: what you thought: in the beginning is just how the Bible starts a story.
what it means: before anything, a dark deep, the Spirit over the waters, and God speaking light into being.
what a scholar hears: bereshit, one word in Hebrew; tohu va-vohu, waste and empty; and light named before the sun exists.

sources.quoted: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep.
And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.

notes: Year two opens: 'the whole book, in order'. Confirm the framing ('not every verse, but every turn of the road') matches the year-two plan.
'Some readers picture a bird hovering over a nest': the Hebrew verb (merachefet) is used of an eagle hovering over its young in Deuteronomy 32:11; confirm wording.
Range of readings of the six days (literal week, poem of order from chaos, etc.) given without ranking; confirm it is fair to young-earth, old-earth and non-literal readers.
'No struggle, no battle': a contrast often drawn with ancient Near Eastern creation stories; the script deliberately does not name them. Confirm.
The Easter Vigil readings (howItsDone) begin with Genesis 1 in the Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran rites; confirm 'many churches'.

Reviewer fix: hook said 'four words in English' for 'in the beginning' (three); corrected. 'The first thing God does in the Bible is speak' softened to 'up close, the first thing we see God do', since 1:1 already says God created; myth item reworded to 'God's first recorded words'.
